table.caption: Price of a movie ticket and tickets sold per day at one theater (invented data for practice)
Hours worked in a week and pay for that week at one part-time job (invented data for practice)

items.q: Label this graph of a market. Price goes up the side, quantity goes across the bottom, and each curve carries its name.

why.correct: Price is on the vertical axis and Quantity on the horizontal axis; the falling curve is D (demand) and the rising one is S (supply). Readers check every label.

items.q: The marked point is where the market starts. Place point X on curve S so that it shows a larger quantity and a higher price than the marked point.

why.correct: A larger quantity is farther right on the horizontal axis, and a higher price is farther up the vertical axis, so X sits up and to the right of the starting point.

items.q: On a graph with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis, which ordered pair plots the row for a price of \$10?

why.correct: An ordered pair lists the horizontal value first: 300 tickets across, then \$10 up.
options: This puts the price first, which would place price on the horizontal axis.
Right: horizontal value (300 tickets) first, vertical value (\$10) second.
Both numbers are the quantity; the price of \$10 is missing.
Both numbers are the price; the 300 tickets are missing.

items.q: What kind of relationship does the table show between the price of a ticket and the number of tickets sold?
options: An inverse relationship: as price rises, tickets sold fall
A direct relationship: as the price rises, tickets sold rise
No relationship: tickets sold do not depend on price
A relationship that rises and then falls

why.correct: Each \$2 rise in price comes with 100 fewer tickets sold, so the two move in opposite directions.
options: Right: the variables move in opposite directions.
In a direct relationship both would rise together; here tickets fall as price rises.
Tickets sold change in every row as price changes.
Tickets sold fall in every row; they never turn back up.

items.q: Using the table, by how many tickets a day do sales fall when the price rises from \$8 to \$12?

why.correct: At \$8 the theater sells 400 tickets and at \$12 it sells 200: $400 - 200 = 200$ fewer tickets.

mistakes.why: That is the change in price (\$12 - \$8). The question asks for the change in tickets, the other column.
You added the two quantities. A change is the new value minus the old one: 400 - 200.

items.q: If the pattern in the table continues, how many tickets a day would the theater sell at a price of \$14?

why.correct: Each \$2 rise cuts sales by 100 tickets, so \$14 brings 200 - 100 = 100.
options: That cuts sales by only 50; the table shows 100 fewer for each \$2.
That is the number sold at \$12, as if sales stopped falling.
That is the number sold at \$10, two steps back.
Right: the pattern is 100 fewer tickets for each \$2.

items.q: As the outdoor temperature rises over a week, a cafe sells fewer cups of hot chocolate. Which statement describes these two variables?
options: They have a direct relationship, moving together
They have no relationship
They have an inverse relationship
Temperature depends on cups sold

why.correct: One rises while the other falls, which is an inverse (negative) relationship.
options: A direct relationship means both rise or both fall together.
Sales change as the temperature changes, so they are related.
Right: higher temperature comes with fewer cups sold.
The cafe sales follow the weather, not the other way round.

items.q: Which pair of variables is most likely to have a direct relationship?
options: The price of a snack and the number of snacks bought
Hours worked in a week and that week's pay
Hours spent on a phone game and hours left for sleep
The price of a bus fare and the number of riders

why.correct: More hours worked bring more pay: both rise together.
options: Buyers usually buy fewer snacks at a higher price, an inverse relationship.
Right: both rise together.
More time on a game leaves less time for sleep, an inverse relationship.
A higher fare usually means fewer riders, an inverse relationship.

items.q: On a graph with hours studied across the bottom and test score up the side, point Q is (0, 40). What does it show?
options: A student who studied 0 hours and scored 40
A student who studied 40 hours and scored 0
A score that rose by 40 points
The average of 0 and 40

why.correct: The first number is the horizontal value (hours studied) and the second the vertical value (score).
options: Right: 0 on the horizontal axis, 40 on the vertical axis.
This reverses the order; the horizontal value comes first.
A single point shows one pair of values, not a change.
An ordered pair is two separate values, not something to average.

items.q: A reader checks your graph for its labeling point. Which features must it have? Select all that apply.
options: A label on the horizontal axis
A label on each curve
A title written above the graph
Each curve drawn in a different color

why.correct: Readers look for every axis and every curve labeled. A title and colors are not scored.
options: Right: each axis must be labeled.
Right: each curve carries its name, such as D or S.
A title is fine but not what earns the point.
Colors do not earn points; handwritten graphs on the exam are in one color.

items.q: A student draws a market graph with Quantity up the side and Price across the bottom, and labels everything else correctly. What happens to the labeling point?
options: It is earned, because both axes carry a label
It is earned if the curves are drawn neatly
It is lost only if the curves are unlabeled too
It is lost, because the axes are swapped from the standard graph

why.correct: A market graph puts Price on the vertical axis and Quantity on the horizontal axis. Swapped axes are wrong axes.
options: A label must be the right one on the right axis, not just present.
Neat curves do not fix swapped axes.
The axes alone are enough to lose the point.
Right: the standard axes are part of the point.

items.q: On a graph with hours worked on the horizontal axis and weekly pay on the vertical axis, a student plots the first row as (60, 5). What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the two values can be written in either order
The point needs a third value for the hourly wage
The order is swapped: the row is the point (5, 60)
The row belongs at the origin, since it is the first one

why.correct: An ordered pair is (horizontal value, vertical value). Hours are horizontal here, so the row is (5, 60). The pair (60, 5) would mean 60 hours of work for 5 dollars.
options: The order matters: (60, 5) and (5, 60) are different points.
A point on a graph is one pair of values, one for each axis.
Right: horizontal value first, so 5 hours, then 60 dollars.
The origin is where both values are zero, and this row is 5 hours and 60 dollars.

items.q: A point is plotted for the 15-hour row. Dashed lines run from it straight down and straight across. Where do they meet the axes?
options: At 15 on the horizontal axis and 180 on the vertical axis
At 180 on the horizontal axis and 15 on the vertical axis
At 15 on both axes, since the row is for 15 hours
At the origin, where the two axes meet each other

why.correct: To read a point, drop a dashed line straight down to the horizontal axis (15 hours) and another straight across to the vertical axis (180 dollars).
options: Right: hours are on the horizontal axis and pay is on the vertical axis.
That swaps the axes: hours are horizontal and pay is vertical.
The line across reaches the vertical axis at the pay for that row, 180 dollars.
Dashed lines from a point go to each axis at the point's own values, not to the origin.

items.q: Which statement describes the relationship in the table and how its points run across the graph?
options: Inverse: the points fall as they move to the right
Direct: the points climb as they move to the right
Inverse: the points climb as they move to the right
Direct: the points fall as they move to the right

why.correct: Hours and pay rise together, which is a direct (positive) relationship. Its points climb to the right.
options: In an inverse relationship one variable falls as the other rises. Here pay rises with hours.
Right: more hours come with more pay, so each point is higher than the one to its left.
Points that climb to the right show a direct relationship, not an inverse one.
Pay rises with hours, so the points climb. Falling points would mean an inverse relationship.

items.q: Where is the origin of a graph, and what does it show?
options: The highest point plotted, where both values are largest
The middle of the graph, where the curves usually cross
The end of the horizontal axis, where its label is written
The corner where the axes meet, where both values are zero

why.correct: The two axes meet at the origin, the corner where both values are zero (or the lowest value shown).
options: The origin is where the axes start, not the highest point.
Where curves cross depends on the curves. The origin is the corner where the axes meet.
The label names the axis's variable. The origin is at the start of both axes.
Right: both number lines start at the origin.

items.q: Which steps correctly plot the point (4, 9)?
options: Start at the origin, move right 9, then move up 4
Start at 4 on the vertical axis, then move right 9
Start at the origin, move right 4, then move up 9
Start at 9 on the horizontal axis, then move up 4

why.correct: The first value is horizontal and the second is vertical: from the origin, move right to 4, then up to 9.
options: That plots (9, 4). The first value in the pair is the horizontal one.
That also plots (9, 4): a vertical value of 4 and a horizontal value of 9.
Right: right to the horizontal value, then up to the vertical value.
That plots (9, 4). The horizontal value is 4, not 9.
